function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow locally (or in a CI environment) to accomplish everything you asked for.  
I’ll walk through the commands you’d run, the files you’d generate, and the final Git workflow.  
Feel free to copy‑paste the snippets into your terminal or editor.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# SSH clone – make sure you have the key set up for git@github.com
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick `tree` or `ls -R` to see the structure:

```bash
tree -L 2
```

Typical output (adjusted to your repo):

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── src/
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

From this we can infer:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `package.json` | Node.js dependencies & scripts |
| `src/index.js` | Main entry point |
| `README.md` | Project description |

### 2.2 Create / update Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Use official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY src ./src

# Expose the port your app listens on (adjust if needed)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and stable.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs.  
> * Exposing port `3000` – change if your app uses a different port.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a `k8s/` directory and add two files: `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to deploy**  
> ```bash
> kubectl apply -f k8s/
> ```

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test   # adjust if you have a test script

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_URL }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD }} | docker login ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_URL }} -u ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
        docker push ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_URL }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Tag latest
      run: |
        docker tag ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_URL }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_URL }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        docker push ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_URL }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `REGISTRY_URL` – e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`  
> * `REGISTRY_USERNAME` – your registry username  
> * `REGISTRY_PASSWORD` – your registry password/token  

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Builds on every push to `main`.  
> * Installs deps, runs tests, builds & pushes Docker image.  
> * Tags the image with the commit SHA and `latest`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/ .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you want to stage everything automatically:

```bash
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **What happens next?**  
> * The GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the push.  
> * It will build the Docker image, push it to your registry, and you’ll have a ready‑to‑deploy image.  
> * You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t nodejs-welcome-test .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests
kubectl apply -f k8s/ --dry-run=client
```

If both commands succeed, you’re good to go!

---

## Recap

| Step | Command / File |
|------|----------------|
| 1 | `git clone ...` |
| 2.1 | Inspect repo (`tree`, `ls`) |
| 2.2 | `Dockerfile` (Node.js) |
| 2.3 | `k8s/deployment.yaml`, `k8s/service.yaml` |
| 2.4 | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| 3 | `git add ...` |
| 4 | `git commit && git push` |

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
